content: Suprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) approved by the FDA for the treatment of intraoperative miosis. Common adverse reactions include burning, stinging, eye discomfort, itching, and redness. For adult patients, the FDA-labeled indication for Suprofen (PROFENAL Ophthalmic Solution) is the inhibition of intraoperative miosis. On the day of surgery, two drops should be instilled into the conjunctival sac at three, two, and one hour prior to surgery. Additionally, two drops may be instilled every four hours while awake on the day preceding surgery. There is limited information regarding off-label use of Suprofen in adults, whether guideline-supported or not. For pediatric patients, there is limited information regarding both FDA-labeled and off-label use of Suprofen. Its safety and effectiveness in pediatric populations have not been established. Suprofen is contraindicated in patients with epithelial herpes simplex keratitis (dendritic keratitis) and in individuals hypersensitive to any component of the medication. Cross-sensitivity to acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) and other NSAIDs is possible, so caution is advised in patients with known sensitivities to these drugs. NSAIDs, including Suprofen, may increase bleeding time due to interference with platelet aggregation. Reports suggest that ocularly applied NSAIDs may increase the bleeding tendency of ocular tissues during surgery. Oral Suprofen has been associated with a syndrome of acute flank pain and reversible renal insufficiency, potentially presenting as acute uric acid nephropathy. This syndrome occurs in approximately 1 in 3500 patients and has been reported with as few as one or two doses of a 200 mg capsule. The total dose of Suprofen applied ophthalmically over two days is significantly lower than a single 200 mg oral dose. Care should be taken to avoid contamination of the solution by not touching the dropper tip to any surface. Patients with a history of herpes simplex keratitis should be closely monitored, as Suprofen is contraindicated in those with active herpes simplex keratitis. The potential for increased ocular bleeding during surgery associated with NSAIDs should also be considered. The most frequent adverse reactions reported in clinical trials include short-duration burning and stinging. Other reported reactions include discomfort, itching, and redness. Approximately 5% of patients experienced allergy, iritis, pain, chemosis, photophobia, irritation, and punctate epithelial staining. No systemic reactions related to therapy were reported in clinical studies, but systemic absorption of ocularly applied drugs is known to occur. NSAIDs have been shown to increase bleeding time by interfering with platelet aggregation, so caution is recommended in patients with bleeding tendencies or those taking anticoagulants. Suprofen is excreted in human milk after a single oral dose, with milk concentrations approximately 1% of plasma levels. Due to potential systemic absorption from topical ocular administration and the lack of established safety in neonates, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing while using PROFENAL. Reproductive studies in animals have shown increased fetal resorption associated with maternal toxicity at higher doses. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, so Suprofen should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Use during late pregnancy should be avoided due to the known effects of NSAIDs on the fetal cardiovascular system, such as closure of the ductus arteriosus. There is no FDA guidance on the use of Suprofen in labor and delivery, geriatric patients, specific gender or racial populations, or patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Additionally, there is no guidance on its use in immunocompromised patients or in females of reproductive potential and males. Suprofen is a phenylalkanoic acid derivative with analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory properties. Its mechanism of action is believed to involve inhibition of the cyclooxygenase enzyme, which is essential for prostaglandin biosynthesis. Prostaglandins are mediators of intraocular inflammation and play a role in the miosis observed during ocular surgery. Clinical studies have shown that PROFENAL inhibits miosis during cataract surgery, although it may interfere with the miotic effect of intraoperatively administered acetylcholine chloride. Nonclinical toxicology studies in mice have shown an increased incidence of benign hepatomas at higher doses. Long-term studies in rats and mice revealed no evidence of carcinogenicity at doses up to 40 mg/kg/day. Suprofen does not appear to have mutagenic potential based on mutagenicity tests. Reproductive studies in rats showed no impairment of fertility at doses up to 40 mg/kg/day, but testicular atrophy/hypoplasia was observed in some animal studies at higher doses. There is limited information regarding the pharmacokinetics, clinical studies, storage, and patient counseling information for Suprofen in the drug label. Overdosage is not expected to cause acute problems, but in cases of accidental ingestion, drinking fluids to dilute the drug is recommended. Chronic overdose information is also limited. Suprofen is available as a 1% ophthalmic solution for topical use. It should be stored at room temperature. There is no established interaction between Suprofen and alcohol, but patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol use while taking this medication.
